content: The term Geneva School refers to two distinct groups: (1) a collective of linguists based in Geneva who were instrumental in the development of modern structural linguistics, and (2) a group of literary theorists and critics who approached their work from a phenomenological perspective. Geneva School of Linguistics The most prominent figure of the Geneva School of Linguistics was Ferdinand de Saussure. Other significant members of this school included Saussure’s colleagues and students, such as Albert Sechehaye, Albert Riedlinger, Sergej Karcevski, and Charles Bally. The most influential linguistic work associated with this school is Cours de linguistique générale (Course in General Linguistics), which represents Saussure’s primary contribution to the field. This book was published posthumously by his students Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye, based on lecture notes from Saussure’s courses delivered in Geneva between 1906 and 1912. Notably, Bally and Sechehaye did not attend these lectures themselves but relied on notes provided by other students, particularly Albert Riedlinger, who contributed the most material. Bally and Sechehaye further developed Saussure’s theories, focusing primarily on linguistic research related to speech. Sechehaye also concentrated on syntactic issues, expanding the scope of Saussure’s foundational ideas. Charles Bally Charles Bally, in addition to editing Saussure’s lectures, made significant contributions to the field of linguistics. Born in Switzerland in 1865, Bally was the son of Jean Gabriel, a teacher, and Henriette, who owned a cloth store. Bally was married three times: first to Valentine Leirens, then to Irma Baptistine Doutre (who was institutionalized in 1915), and finally to Alice Bellicot. Bally studied classical languages and literature in Geneva from 1883 to 1885. He continued his education in Berlin from 1886 to 1889, where he earned a PhD. After completing his studies, he worked as a private tutor for the royal family of Greece from 1889 to 1893. Upon returning to Geneva, Bally taught at a business school starting in 1893 and later at a grammar school (Progymnasium) from 1913 to 1939. Concurrently, he served as a Privatdozent (PD) at the University of Geneva from 1893 to 1913. From 1913 to 1939, Bally held a professorship in general linguistics and comparative Indo-Germanic studies, succeeding Ferdinand de Saussure in this role. Bally’s work extended beyond linguistics to include studies on subjectivity in the French language, the crisis in the French language, and language education. Today, he is recognized as a founding figure in the linguistic theories of style and is highly regarded for his contributions to phraseology. Notable Works by Charles Bally: Traité de stylistique française (1909) Le Langage et la Vie (1913) Linguistique générale et linguistique française (1932) Recommended Literature on Bally’s Theories: G. Redard, Bibliographie chronologique des publications de Charles Bally, in Cahiers Ferdinand de Saussure 36, 1982, pp. 25–41. W. Hellmann, Charles Bally (1988). S. Durrer, Introduction à la linguistique de Charles Bally (1998). Geneva School of Literary Criticism The term Geneva School is also applied to a group of literary critics active during the 1950s and 1960s. Key figures in this group included the Belgian critic Georges Poulet, the French critic Jean-Pierre Richard, and Swiss critics Marcel Raymond, Albert Béguin, Jean Rousset, and Jean Starobinski. Other critics, such as Emil Staiger, Gaston Bachelard, and J. Hillis Miller, are sometimes associated with this group. Emerging from the traditions of Russian Formalism and phenomenology (notably the work of Edmund Husserl), the Geneva School employed phenomenological methods to analyze literary works. They viewed literature as a representation of the deep structures of an author’s consciousness and their relationship to the real world. However, they avoided biographical criticism, focusing instead on the work of art itself. They treated literary works as organic wholes, interpreting them as subjective representations of reality (a concept akin to the German Lebenswelt). Their analyses often emphasized recurring themes and images, particularly those related to time, space, and the interactions between the self and others. Notes and References Terry Eagleton, Literary Theory: An Introduction (1983), ISBN 0-8166-1241-2. For this section, see Eagleton, pp. 58–60.
